repo.name: neovim

body:
Closes #41187.

### Problem
It is common to construct a position or range from the return values of either `nvim_buf_get_extmark_by_id()` or `nvim_buf_get_extmarks()`. This is verbose since `vim.pos.extmark()` and `vim.range.extmark()` do not accept these types.

### Solution
Add support for directly passing these types to `.extmark()` constructors.

---

~~There are no general tests for `vim.pos.extmark()` or `vim.range.extmark()`, so I didn't add any tests. Let me know if I should add tests for both this and the original case.~~ Added tests!

~~I wasn't completely sure if it was agreed on in #41187 to implement this yet, but I figured writing an implementation couldn't hurt, especially because it was simple.~~

@ofseed

comment_data.body:
```suggestion
---@overload fun(buf: integer, extmark: vim.api.keyset.get_extmark_item): vim.Pos, vim.Pos?
```

I think when an extmark has `end_row` and `end_col`, we could make it return both `pos`, which conveniently covers the use case where we want to construct a `vim.Pos` from an extmark's end position. Besides, this could help reduce potential pitfalls.

comment_regular_data.body:
> given that `vim.range(...)` and `vim.range.extmark(...)` do largely the same thing

They don't just largely do the same thing, they actually do the exact same thing. Perhaps it makes since to remove the original `vim.{pos,range}.extmark(...)` forms in favor of `vim.{pos,range}()`? Consider that `vim.*.extmark()` is currently unused and untested. It will also make it easier to document this new form (with multiple returns) instead of having to cram this information into an `@overload`.

> Perhaps it makes since to remove the original vim.{pos,range}.extmark(...) forms in favor of vim.{pos,range}()?

I thibk it's better to keep it for consistency, since each position type (LSP, cursor, mark, extmark) has a dedicated function to create a `vim.Pos` from `row` and `col`. That was the original reason for its existence.

> each position type (LSP, cursor, mark, extmark) has a dedicated function to create a `vim.Pos` from `row` and `col`

`vim.pos.lsp()` does not have this.

> vim.pos.lsp() does not have this.

Not entirely. Since LSP positions are bound to a position encoding, converting an LSP position + encoding into `vim.Pos` is practically the same as constructing a `vim.Pos` from `row`, `col`, and `encoding`.

Doesn't the same apply to constructing an extmark from an `vim.api.keyset.get_extmark_item`? They both take a specialized table which represents a position and convert it to a `vim.Pos`.

Anyway, if you think the original form should say, I can definitely keep it. I might swap which one is the default and which one is the overloaded version, though, just to improve the docs.

> Doesn't the same apply to constructing an extmark from an vim.api.keyset.get_extmark_item? They both take a specialized table which represents a position and convert it to a vim.Pos.

An LSP `Position` is already a position, whereas an extmark isn't. The position encoding is metadata that directly changes what `line` and `character` actually point to, while extra fields in an extmark table don't affect `row` and `col`.

Put another way, even a function taking raw LSP fields (like `vim.pos.lsp(buf, line, character)`) would still need `position_encoding`, or the same coordinates could mean different things. Then the only difference from what we have now is whether it's wrapped in a table.

In fact, whether to wrap row and col in a table is a topic,e.g., using `vim.pos.cursor(buf, {row = ..., col = ...})` instead of the current signature. Ultimately, we decided to handle each case based on its specific context.

My takeaway is that `vim.pos.<type>` essentially provides two variant:

1. Constructing a `vim.Pos` directly from `row` and `col` under different indexing semantics (our original intent).
2. Providing a convenience helper to cut down on boilerplate (first `vim.pos.cursor`, now `vim.pos.extmark`).

I mentioned earlier that I also considered a shorthand for extmarks, but my idea is `vim.pos.extmark(buf, id)` to skip calling `nvim_buf_get_extmark_by_id`, this
 matches how `vim.pos.cursor(win)` saves an `nvim_win_get_current_cursor` call. (Maybe worth reconsidering that signature?) I'm just not sure how useful it actually is.

Finally, `vim.pos.lsp()` just happens to fulfill both purposes in a single signature by coincidence.

> `vim.pos.extmark(buf, id)` to skip calling `nvim_buf_get_extmark_by_id`

I like it, and it would be trivial to add to this PR.

Edit: would also require a namespace parameter (and therefore *another* overload). Best saved for another PR imo.

Made a lot of improvements:
- `{extmark}` accepts `nvim_buf_get_extmark_by_id()` return value in addition to `nvim_buf_get_extmarks()`.
- Deduplicated code.
- Improved the docs.
- Actually wrote tests for `.extmarks()`!
